title: assistant extension marketplace prototype notes
body:
High-level idea

Build a lightweight "assistant extension marketplace" for Redwood-hosted assistant integrations: a place where developers and partners can publish small, sandboxed extensions that attach to Redwood responses (pre-/post-processing, tool adapters, domain enrichers). The goal is to accelerate customer feature velocity (add capabilities without modifying app logic) while keeping control of execution, cost, and data residency.

Why this could matter
- Many customers want to add small capabilities (e.g., calendar lookup, domain-specific rewriters, profanity filters, custom rerankers) without building full server-side toolchains.
- A curated marketplace lowers integration friction and creates potential for partner ecosystem and monetization (premium extensions, verified partners).
- Redwood can offer curated, performance-profiled extensions that run safely in our runtime or as local adapters in private deployments.

Primary user personas
- Product engineer at an early-stage startup: wants an out-of-box invoice-parser extension to speed up a feature demo.
- Platform engineer at enterprise: needs an approved data-sanitizer extension that meets compliance and can run inside VPC private deployments.
- Solutions engineer/partner: wants to publish a paid connector (e.g., Salesforce summarizer) that customers can install.

Core goals (north stars)
1) Installable extensions with clear trust boundary: users can opt-in per-project and restrict data flows.
2) Small runtime cost and predictable latency impact (extensions should have SLAs/cost profiles).
3) Developer experience: discover, configure, version, and test extensions via Console and API.
4) Safety and governance: publishing workflow with vetting, automated static checks, runtime sandboxing, and telemetry.

What an extension looks like (concept)
- Manifest: metadata (name, owner, version, inputs, outputs, cost profile, compat models, deployment modes supported).
- Hook points: pre-prompt (modify prompt), post-gen (transform output), embedding-layer (augment embeddings), rerank hook, or tool-invoker adapter.
- Execution modes: hosted-sandbox (Redwood-managed secure runtime), delegated-adapter (customer-hosted adapter behind oauth/URL), private-only (on-prem package reference).

Example user stories
- As an app engineer, I can search the marketplace, read docs and reviews, and install an "expense-normalizer" to my project in 2 clicks.
- As a security lead, I can see the extension manifest and enforce a policy that prevents any extension from calling external URLs unless approved.
- As a partner developer, I can publish a paid version of my extension with a trial period and monthly billing.
- As a product manager, I can pick a fallback behavior: if an extension times out, either continue without it or route to a cheaper variant.

Acceptance criteria (MVP)
- Console: listing + detail page for extensions, install button, simple config form.
- API: endpoints to list, install, enable/disable per-project, and pass config.
- Runtime: implement pre-prompt and post-gen hooks for hosted-sandbox extensions with a 500ms median additional latency target and 99% under 2s for small transforms.
- Security: static manifest checks, role-based controls to restrict install, and telemetry showing data flows.

Success metrics (first 6 months)
- 20% of new hosted projects install at least one extension within first 30 days.
- Average time-to-ship feature reduced by 30% for projects using extensions (self-reported).
- 2 partner-published extensions with paid tiers onboarded.

Tech considerations and constraints
- Sandboxing: use language-agnostic WASM for extension runtime or a constrained microservice container model. Evaluate trade-offs: WASM gives portability and strong isolation but may limit some libraries; containers easier for complex partners but heavier.
- Observability: attribute extension CPU/memory and per-request timing to token-level traces in Console.
- Data residency: for private deployments, provide a mechanism to run extension code inside customer VPC (deployable bundle or connector) and mark extension as private-only.
- Config and secrets: support project-level secrets for extension connectors; ensure KMS-backed storage and strict RBAC.
- Cost model: extensions should expose a cost profile (e.g., per-call CPU multiplier or external call cost) so billing can be predictable.

Privacy & compliance checklist (initial)
- Manifest declares whether PII may leave boundary.
- Hosted extensions must attest to no persistent storage of customer prompt content unless explicitly enabled.
- Review worksheet for SOC2/ISO-relevant behavior for partner extensions.

UX quick flow (Console)
1) Marketplace browse -> filter by category (data-connectors, NLU preprocessors, domain models).
2) Click extension -> view docs, latency/cost badge, reviews, supported models, install.
3) Install -> modal to choose config and data permissions -> sandbox test run with sample prompt.
4) Enable -> extension appears in project route config, priority order for hooks, can be toggled on/off.

Rollout plan (phases)
- Phase 0 (R&D): prototype hosted-sandbox pre/post hooks with 3 internal extensions (profanity filter, date normalizer, currency converter).
- Phase 1 (alpha): closed alpha with 4 customers + partner beta; add manifest schema, Console listing pages.
- Phase 2 (public beta): open marketplace, partner publishing onboarding, billing integration for paid extensions.

Open questions / risks
- Billing granularity: meter extension CPU vs. per-call vs. combined. How to show transparent cost to users?
- Liability for partner extensions: what is Redwood’s responsibility if an extension returns wrong legal advice or leaks? Need legal review and T&Cs.
- Performance: how many chained extensions can we support before latency SLOs break? Need backpressure policies.
- Private deployments: how to manage private extension lifecycle (updates/patches) in customer environments safely?

Next immediate experiments (next 2 sprints)
- Implement a minimal pre-prompt hook in runtime and wire up a Console toggle for a single project.
- Build manifest schema v0 and a simple validation tool to catch network-IO flags, required fields.
- Run internal perf test: measure median added latency for a 100-char transformation in hosted-sandbox.

Notes to self
- Keep MVP scope tiny: only pre- and post- hooks at first; avoid embedding-layer and reranking until we have stable security patterns.
- Lean on WASM if it's feasible for standard transforms — makes private deployment simpler.
- Coordinate with legal and security early for partner onboarding checklist.

Potential low-effort extensions to seed marketplace
- profanity / PII masker
- canonical date/amount normalizer
- domain glossary replacer (replace brand names with canonical forms)
- simple SRL-based intent extractor (lightweight deterministic rules)

End of notes.
